summary.title: Scenario 3
summary.description:
A healthcare organisation has deployed a microservices-based patient management system. The system comprises the following services:

• Patient Portal: A web frontend through which patients access their medical records and book appointments.

Threat Modelling Assignment Information Security

• Identity Service: Handles authentication and authorisation using OAuth 2.0 and issues JSON Web Tokens (JWTs).
• Medical Records Service: Stores and retrieves patient records; communicates with the identity service to verify tokens.
• Appointment Service: Manages appointment scheduling; reads patient data from the medical records service.
• Notification Service: Sends appointment reminders via SMS and email using third-party providers.
• API Gateway: Routes all inbound requests to the appropriate backend service.
All inter-service communication occurs over an internal network. The patient portal and the API gateway are exposed to the public internet.

threats.title: Compromised Notification Service Pivoting to Internal Services
threats.description: The Notification Service has the weakest security posture — it integrates with external third-party providers (SMS, email) making it the most exposed internal service. If an attacker exploits a vulnerability in a third-party SDK used by the Notification Service, they gain code execution inside the internal network. From there, they can make direct API calls to Medical Records Service or Identity Service — services that may implicitly trust internal network traffic — effectively elevating from a low-value notification service to full records access.
threats.mitigation: Notification Service should only be able to communicate with the services it strictly needs (Appointment Service inbound only), enforced by internal firewall rules. Run each service with minimum required permissions (principle of least privilege). Treat the Notification Service as semi-untrusted given its third-party exposure. Standard: NIST 800-53 AC-6, SC-7, ISO 27001 A.13.1, Zero Trust Architecture principles.

threats.title: API Gateway Request Parameter Injection
threats.description: An attacker crafts malicious requests to the API Gateway with manipulated parameters — e.g. changing patient_id=123 to patient_id=456 in a records request. If the API Gateway forwards parameters without validation and downstream services trust them without re-authorizing against the JWT claims, the attacker accesses another patient's data (IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference).
threats.mitigation: API Gateway must validate and sanitize all inputs before forwarding. Downstream services must re-verify authorization — the Medical Records Service should cross-check that the patient_id in the request matches the subject claim in the JWT, never trusting the raw parameter alone. Standard: OWASP Top 10 A01, NIST 800-53 SI-10.

threats.title: JWT Claims Leakage via Verbose Error Responses
threats.description: If the API Gateway or any internal service returns verbose error messages (e.g. stack traces, decoded JWT payloads, internal service URLs) to the frontend on failed requests, an attacker can probe endpoints with malformed inputs to harvest internal architecture details, patient ID formats, and JWT structure — all of which accelerate further attacks.
threats.mitigation: Implement a global error handling layer at the API Gateway that strips internal details and returns only generic error codes to the client. Internal error details go to logs only, never to the response body. Standard: OWASP Top 10 A05 (Security Misconfiguration), NIST 800-53 SI-11.

threats.title: Patient Portal Phishing / Credential Harvesting
threats.description: An attacker clones the Patient Portal UI and hosts it on a lookalike domain (e.g. patient-porta1.hospital.com). Patients submit real credentials to the fake site. Since there's no MFA, the attacker immediately uses harvested credentials to log into the real portal and access medical records.
threats.mitigation: Enforce Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for all patient logins. Implement DMARC/DKIM/SPF on the hospital domain to prevent email-based phishing. Add HSTS preloading so browsers refuse non-HTTPS connections. Standard: NIST 800-53 IA-2, ISO 27001 A.9.4.

threats.title: JWT Forgery via Weak Signing Key
threats.description: If the Identity Service signs JWTs with a weak or hardcoded secret (e.g. secret123), an attacker can brute-force the signing key offline using tools like hashcat against a captured token. They then forge a JWT with elevated claims (e.g. "role": "admin" or another patient's ID) and make API requests impersonating any user. In a healthcare context this means unauthorized access to any patient's medical records — a critical HIPAA violation.
threats.mitigation: Use RS256 (asymmetric signing) instead of HS256 — the private key signs, services only hold the public key for verification, so there's nothing to brute-force. Rotate keys regularly. Standard: OWASP Top 10 A07 (Identification and Authentication Failures), NIST 800-53 IA-5.

threats.title: Patient Records Exposed via Unencrypted Internal Traffic
threats.description: The assignment states inter-service communication occurs over an internal network — but internal doesn't mean encrypted. If services communicate over plain HTTP internally, an attacker who gains a foothold on any internal host (e.g. via a compromised Notification Service dependency) can sniff traffic and intercept patient medical records in plaintext. In a microservices environment, lateral movement between services makes this a high-value attack path.
threats.mitigation: Enforce TLS for all inter-service communication even on the internal network — adopt a zero-trust posture. Encrypt the Patient Records DB at rest using AES-256. Standard: NIST 800-53 SC-8, SC-28, ISO 27001 A.10.1, OWASP Top 10 A02 (Cryptographic Failures).

threats.title: Notification Service Abuse via Appointment Spam
threats.description: An authenticated but malicious patient creates thousands of appointments in rapid succession, each triggering the Notification Service to send SMS/email reminders. This exhausts third-party provider API quotas (SMS credits, email rate limits), causing legitimate notifications to fail. It also drives up operational costs significantly.
threats.mitigation: Implement rate limiting on appointment creation per user (e.g. max 10 per hour). Add async queuing (e.g. RabbitMQ, SQS) between Appointment Service and Notification Service to decouple and throttle outbound notification volume. Standard: NIST 800-53 SC-5, OWASP Top 10 A04 (Insecure Design).

threats.title: Medical Record Modification by Compromised Internal Service
threats.description: The Appointment Service reads patient data from the Medical Records Service. If the Appointment Service is compromised (e.g. via a dependency vulnerability), an attacker could send forged write requests to the Medical Records Service to alter diagnoses, medication dosages, or allergy records. Since inter-service communication is on an internal network, there may be implicit trust with no per-request authorization checks. Tampered medical records could directly endanger patient lives.
threats.mitigation: Enforce mutual TLS (mTLS) between all internal services so each service cryptographically proves its identity. Medical Records Service must require explicit write authorization even from internal callers — no implicit trust. Standard: NIST 800-53 SC-8, ISO 27001 A.13.2, OWASP Top 10 A01 (Broken Access Control).

threats.title: Insufficient Audit Logging Across Services
threats.description: A malicious insider (e.g. a rogue nurse) queries patient records they have no clinical reason to access. If each microservice logs independently without a centralized audit trail, or if logs are stored locally and can be deleted by the same process that writes them, there's no reliable way to prove who accessed what and when. In healthcare, this directly violates audit requirements under HIPAA and ISO 27001.
threats.mitigation: Implement a centralized, tamper-evident audit logging system (e.g. write-once log store, SIEM integration). Every read/write to Patient Records DB and Appointments DB must emit a structured log event with service identity, user JWT subject, timestamp, and operation. Standard: NIST 800-53 AU-2, AU-9, ISO 27001 A.12.4, HIPAA Audit Controls.
